content: Enoxaparin sodium was administered to 25 healthy male and female subjects at concentrations of 100 mg/mL or 200 mg/mL. The pharmacokinetic profiles observed are as follows: Distribution: The volume of distribution for anti-Factor Xa activity is approximately 4.3 liters. Elimination: After intravenous (IV) administration, the total body clearance of enoxaparin is 26 mL/min. Following IV dosing of enoxaparin labeled with the gamma-emitter 99mTc, 40% of the radioactivity and 8–20% of the anti-Factor Xa activity were recovered in the urine within 24 hours. The elimination half-life, based on anti-Factor Xa activity, is approximately 4.5 hours after a single subcutaneous (SC) dose and extends to about 7 hours after repeated dosing. Significant anti-Factor Xa activity remains in the plasma for approximately 12 hours following a 40 mg SC once-daily dose. After SC administration, the apparent clearance (CL/F) of enoxaparin is approximately 15 mL/min. Metabolism: Enoxaparin sodium is primarily metabolized in the liver through desulfation and/or depolymerization, resulting in lower molecular weight species with significantly reduced biological activity. Renal Clearance: Active fragments account for approximately 10% of the administered dose cleared renally, while total renal excretion of both active and inactive fragments represents about 40% of the dose. Nonclinical Toxicology Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility: No long-term animal studies have been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of enoxaparin. Enoxaparin was not mutagenic in in vitro tests, including the Ames test, mouse lymphoma cell forward mutation test, human lymphocyte chromosomal aberration test, or in vivo rat bone marrow chromosomal aberration test. Enoxaparin did not affect fertility or reproductive performance in male and female rats at SC doses up to 20 mg/kg/day (141 mg/m²/day). The maximum human dose in clinical trials was 2.0 mg/kg/day (78 mg/m²/day for an average body weight of 70 kg and height of 170 cm, with a body surface area of 1.8 m²). Animal Toxicology and Pharmacology: A single SC dose of 46.4 mg/kg enoxaparin was lethal to rats. Symptoms of acute toxicity included ataxia, reduced motility, dyspnea, cyanosis, and coma. Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology Teratology Studies: Studies in pregnant rats and rabbits at SC doses of enoxaparin up to 30 mg/kg/day (211 mg/m²/day in rats and 410 mg/m²/day in rabbits) showed no evidence of teratogenic effects or fetotoxicity. Clinical Studies Prophylaxis of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) Following Abdominal Surgery in Patients at Risk for Thromboembolic Complications: Patients at risk included those over 40 years of age, obese, undergoing surgery under general anesthesia lasting more than 30 minutes, or with additional risk factors such as malignancy or a history of DVT or pulmonary embolism (PE). In a double-blind, parallel-group study of 1116 patients undergoing elective cancer surgery of the gastrointestinal, urological, or gynecological tract, 1115 patients were treated. The mean age was 67 years (range: 32–97 years), with 52.7% men and 47.3% women. Patients were predominantly Caucasian (98%). Lovenox 40 mg SC once daily, initiated 2 hours before surgery and continued for up to 12 days post-surgery, was comparable to heparin 5000 U every 8 hours SC in reducing the risk of DVT. Prophylaxis of DVT Following Hip or Knee Replacement Surgery: Lovenox has been shown to reduce the risk of postoperative DVT following hip or knee replacement surgery. In a double-blind study, Lovenox 30 mg every 12 hours SC was compared to placebo in patients undergoing hip replacement. A total of 100 patients were randomized, and all were treated. The mean age was 67.1 years (range: 41–84 years), with 45% men and 55% women. Treatment was initiated 12–24 hours after surgery and continued for 10–14 days. The incidence of proximal and total DVT was significantly lower for Lovenox compared to placebo. In another double-blind, multicenter study, three dosing regimens of Lovenox were compared in patients undergoing hip replacement. A total of 572 patients were randomized, and 568 were treated. The mean age was 64.7 years (range: 31–88 years), with 63% men and 37% women. Treatment was initiated within two days after surgery and continued for 7–11 days. There was no significant difference between the 30 mg every 12 hours and 40 mg once-daily regimens. In a study of extended prophylaxis for patients undergoing hip replacement surgery, patients were treated with Lovenox 40 mg SC, initiated up to 12 hours before surgery, for the prevention of postoperative DVT. At the end of the perioperative period, all patients underwent bilateral venography. In a double-blind design, patients without venous thromboembolic disease were randomized to a post-discharge regimen of either Lovenox 40 mg once daily SC or placebo for three weeks. A total of 179 patients were randomized in the double-blind phase, and all were treated. The mean age was 69.4 years (range: 47–87 years), with 57% men and 43% women. The incidence of DVT during extended prophylaxis was significantly lower for Lovenox compared to placebo.
